results.title: New Report Published to Help Georgia Businesses and ...
results.content:
ATLANTA – Today, the Georgia Chamber of Commerce announced the publication of Tariffs Briefing: April 2025 - New U.S. Tariffs + Potential Georgia Impact, a report written to help Georgia businesses and communities prepare for the new tariff measures announced by the Trump Administration. The measures mark a significant shift in U.S. trade policy– including across-the-board import tariffs and targeted duties on specific goods – with implications for Georgia’s small businesses, manufacturers, [...] Supply chain networks and key trade-off points, such as Georgia’s coastal and inland ports, may face significant challenges as some consumers and producers attempt to stockpile, and as businesses look to jointly re-organize supply chain structures.
 Tariffs on specific imports, especially metals and manufacturing components, are reported to significantly impact Georgia and U.S. based company’s margins and may push smaller companies out of profitability entirely. [...] The publication of the report is the latest effort to support the Georgia business community in the quickly evolving global trade landscape. In February, the Georgia Chamber launched its Global Business Subcommittee, to provide insights, coordination, and advocacy for Georgia’s agriculture, business, and industry partners invested in international trade.  
  
A copy of the report, Tariffs Briefing: April 2025 - New U.S. Tariffs + Potential Georgia Impact, is available by clicking here.

results.title: Chain Reaction: US Tariffs and Global Supply Chains
results.content: Punitive targets: The administration will continue to use tariffs as a punitive tool, typified by US duties on India for Russian oil purchases and on Brazil for the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro. [...] Supply chains tend to move when goods can be manufactured in countries with lower “landed costs”—the cost of production plus shipping, customs duties, and insurance. Tariffs directly impact these calculations, which helps explain why US imports from China declined after the US imposed Section 301 tariffs on $550 billion of imports from China in 2017 (Figure 1). Transshipment played a role, but it only explains part of shifting trade flows over the period. Crucially, manufacturing capacity [...] incentives. The same is true for apparel and household goods, given India’s established manufacturing capacity and US companies’ commitment to source more from India in these categories. Regardless of how negotiations with the US evolve, India is likely to expand exports of solar PV to the US, due to high anti-dumping/countervailing duties on the other top suppliers in Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Cambodia.

results.content:
Foreign trade zones: Manufacture domestically while deferring or reducing duties based on the final product classification.
 First sale rule: Pay duties based on the manufacturer or middleman price (rather than the importer price).

## Tariff Resources

 Harmonized Tariff Schedule: View exempt products (updated regularly).
 U.S. Customs and Border Protection Centers of Excellence and Expertise (industry-specific):
  + Ask questions, such as how tariffs apply to specific industries. [...] Reshoring: Consider automation opportunities and domestic suppliers (including those who can expand their production).
 Nearshoring: Take advantage of duty-free imports through Mexico.
 Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States Chapter 98 and Chapter 99: Eliminate or reduce duties for qualifying products.
 Bonded warehouses: Store imported products while deferring duties until they leave the facility (quarterly harbor maintenance fees apply).
